lead: Bottom-up parsers read a token string and reduce handles until the start symbol appears. This unit builds LR tables by hand: LR(0) items, SLR, LR(1), LALR, and the YACC tool that automates the last step. After it you can trace a shift-reduce parse, construct an LR automaton, fill a parsing table, and explain why a grammar is or is not SLR, LR(1) or LALR.
about: This unit moves from the stack-and-input view of bottom-up parsing to table-driven LR parsers. Chapter 3.1 shows shift-reduce parsing, handles and handle pruning, with a short treatment of operator precedence. Chapter 3.2 builds LR(0) item sets with closure and goto and turns them into an LR automaton. Chapter 3.3 uses FOLLOW sets to fill SLR tables. Chapter 3.4 adds lookaheads to get canonical LR(1) parsers. Chapter 3.5 merges LR(1) states with the same core to get LALR, the usual practical choice. Chapter 3.6 shows how YACC builds such a parser from a grammar file. After the unit you can build and debug LR tables for small grammars and read a YACC specification.

chapters.idea: A bottom-up parser shifts tokens onto a stack and reduces a handle, the right-hand side that reverses one step of a rightmost derivation.
chapters.depth: Cover the shift-reduce parser model with stack, input and $ end marker; shift, reduce, accept and error actions; handles and handle pruning; why the handle is the rightmost reducible substring. Trace at least one string over an expression grammar. Cover operator precedence parsing, LEADING and TRAILING sets, and the precedence matrix; only a few universities teach this now, so keep it short and show one matrix. Name shift/reduce and reduce/reduce conflicts. Some syllabi call handle pruning 'reduction of the right sentential form'.

figure.title: Shift-reduce trace for id + id * id
figure.aria: Stack contents after selected shift and reduce steps for the input id + id * id, with the reduced handle marked.

chapters.example: Grammar: E → E + T | T, T → T * F | F, F → id. Parse the string id + id * id with a shift-reduce parser; show stack, input, action, and the handle at each reduction. Then write LEADING and TRAILING for E, T and F and the precedence relation between + and *.
chapters.trap: A handle is not just any right-hand side: it must match the production used in the reverse rightmost derivation. Also, a shift-reduce parser is nondeterministic unless a table or precedence relation decides the action.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2: context-free grammars, derivations, rightmost derivations, parse trees.
chapters.leave: LL(1) tables and predictive parsing to Unit 2; semantic actions to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: LR(0) items record how far the dot has moved through a production; closure and goto build a finite automaton whose states drive the parser.
chapters.depth: Cover LR(0) items, dot notation, closure of an item set, goto on a grammar symbol, and the canonical collection of item sets. Build the LR automaton and the ACTION/GOTO table with shift, reduce, accept and error. Show why LR(0) tables can have shift/reduce and reduce/reduce conflicts. Some syllabi call this 'LR(0) item set construction' or 'canonical LR(0) collection'.

figure.aria: LR(0) automaton for S → C C and C → c C | d, with state I0 as start and state I5 as the reduce state for S → C C.

chapters.example: Grammar: S → C C, C → c C | d. Compute closure(I0), all goto sets, the LR(0) automaton, and the LR(0) parsing table. State whether the grammar is LR(0).
chapters.trap: Closure adds items only when the dot is before a nonterminal, and it does not move the dot. Goto moves the dot past one symbol. Mixing the two is the common error.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.1; Unit 2 grammar and derivation basics.
chapters.leave: FOLLOW sets and SLR table construction to Chapter 3.3; error recovery to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: SLR resolves LR(0) reduce actions by allowing a reduction only when the next token is in FOLLOW of the production's left-hand side.
chapters.depth: Cover FIRST and FOLLOW use in SLR, the SLR(1) table construction, and worked conflicts that LR(0) cannot solve. Show a grammar that is SLR but not LR(0). Some syllabi call it 'Simple LR' or 'SLR(1)'; the '1' means one lookahead token.

figure.title: SLR table for E' → E, E → E + T | T, T → id
figure.aria: SLR table rows for six states and columns for id, plus, dollar, E and T, with accept and one reduce entry marked.

chapters.example: Grammar: E' → E, E → E + T | T, T → id. Compute FOLLOW sets and build the SLR(1) parsing table for the string id + id. Show the accept entry and the reduce entries.
chapters.trap: SLR uses FOLLOW of the left-hand side of the reduce production, not the lookahead attached to an LR item. A grammar can be SLR even when its LR(0) table has a conflict.
chapters.leave: Canonical LR(1) lookaheads to Chapter 3.4; LALR merging to Chapter 3.5.

chapters.idea: Canonical LR(1) items carry a lookahead terminal, so a reduction is allowed only for that lookahead and many SLR conflicts disappear.
chapters.depth: Cover LR(1) items [A → α . β, a], closure with lookahead, goto, the canonical collection, and the LR(1) table. Show the closure rule that adds FIRST(βa) to lookaheads. Work the classic grammar that is LR(1) but not SLR. Some syllabi call it 'CLR' or 'canonical LR'.

figure.aria: Canonical LR(1) automaton for S → L = R | R, L → * R | id, R → L, with state I2 holding the shift-reduce conflict of SLR.

chapters.example: Grammar: S → L = R | R, L → * R | id, R → L. Show that the SLR table has a shift/reduce conflict in the state containing S → L . = R and R → L .; then build the LR(1) item sets and table that remove the conflict.
chapters.trap: The lookahead belongs to the item and is propagated through closure using FIRST of the remaining symbols. Do not use FOLLOW of the left-hand side as in SLR.
chapters.leave: State merging and LALR tables to Chapter 3.5; YACC implementation to Chapter 3.6.

chapters.idea: LALR merges LR(1) states that have the same core, keeping lookaheads, so it has LR(0)-size tables but more power than SLR.
chapters.depth: Cover the core of an LR(1) state, merging states with the same core, union of lookaheads, and the possible reduce/reduce conflict introduced by merging. Show a grammar that is LR(1) but not LALR. Compare state counts: LR(0) and LALR have the same number of states. Some syllabi call it 'LookAhead LR' or 'LALR(1)'.

figure.title: Merging LR(1) states to LALR
figure.aria: Two LR(1) states with the same core merge into one LALR state, creating a reduce/reduce conflict on d and e.

chapters.example: Grammar: S → a A d | b B d | a B e | b A e, A → c, B → c. Build the LR(1) states after c; they have the same core but different lookaheads. Merge them into one LALR state and show the reduce/reduce conflict on d and e.
chapters.trap: Merging can combine A → c., d with B → c., e and create a reduce/reduce conflict. LALR is not always as strong as canonical LR(1).
chapters.leave: Parser generators and conflict reports to Chapter 3.6; code generation to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: YACC reads a grammar with semantic actions and precedence declarations and writes a C parser that uses LALR tables.
chapters.depth: Cover the YACC file structure: declarations, %token, grammar rules, semantic actions, %left/%right/%nonassoc, and the lex interface yylex(). Explain how YACC reports shift/reduce and reduce/reduce conflicts and how precedence resolves them. Mention bison as a compatible generator. Keep the example small: expression calculator.

figure.title: YACC build path
figure.aria: YACC reads calc.y, writes y.tab.c, the C compiler builds the parser executable, and the parser reads tokens.

chapters.example: Write a YACC specification for expressions with +, *, parentheses and integer constants. Use %left '+' '-'; %left '*' '/'; and show the grammar rules and semantic actions that build values. Explain how YACC resolves the expression conflict.
chapters.trap: Precedence declarations resolve conflicts by assigned levels and associativity; they do not rewrite the grammar. Without them YACC defaults a shift/reduce conflict to shift.
chapters.leave: Detailed code generation to Unit 6; symbol table and type checking to Unit 4 and Unit 5.
